title: PROVE: Training-Free Prompt Recovery using Verifiable Evidence

paper.title: PROVE: Training-Free Prompt Recovery using Verifiable Evidence
paper.abstract: Abstract Modern text-to-image models can generate highly realistic images from natural-language prompts, while recent advances in prompt inversion have made it increasingly feasible to recover those prompts from generated outputs, raising new concerns for copyright protection and content ownership. As prompt marketplaces emerge, recovered prompts can enable both the unauthorized reproduction and redistribution of copyrighted creative works, and the exposure of the prompts that encode an artist’s creative recipe in AI-generated content. Existing prompt inversion methods rely on gradient-based optimization, autoregressive captioning, or reinforcement learning. However, optimization-based methods often produce unreadable prompts, captioning methods hallucinate unverified details, and RL-based approaches frequently overfit to specific generators while introducing evaluation circularity. We introduce PROVE (Prompt Recovery with Verified Evidence), a training-free, black-box prompt inversion attack that reconstructs prompts by composing verifiable scene descriptions rather than optimizing token sequences, targeting both original copyrighted works and AI-generated content. The resulting prompts are fully auditable, with every recovered claim grounded in explicit image evidence, and are formalized through a precision-constrained recall maximization objective. Across MS-COCO, Flickr30K, and Lexica, using state-of-the-art text-to-image generators, PROVE consistently outperforms optimization, captioning, and RL-based baselines on image similarity (DINO, LPIPS) and text-image alignment (CLIP), without any training, generator access, or fine-tuning, demonstrating a stronger and more practical prompt inversion attack.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: Text-to-image generation has been transformed by diffusion- and flow-based models such as Stable Diffusion ( Esser et al. 2024 ) , DALL-E ( Ramesh et al. 2021 ) , FLUX ( Labs et al. 2025 ) , and Imagen ( Saharia et al. 2022 ) . These models can synthesize highly realistic images from natural-language descriptions, with image quality and fidelity largely determined by their ability to interpret user prompts. This capability has democratized image creation, editing, and content generation, enabling non-experts to produce sophisticated visual content through simple textual instructions. However, the same accessibility introduces significant security, safety, and intellectual property concerns. Prompt manipulation and adversarial prompting can facilitate harmful generation, including the creation of copyrighted derivatives and other forms of misuse ( Bariach et al. 2024 ) . MS-COCO Lexica Original PROVE Original PROVE Figure 1: PROVE regenerations of a real MS-COCO image and an AI-generated image from a Lexica prompt. The emergence of prompt marketplaces, where carefully engineered prompts are shared or sold ( Shen et al. 2024 ; Jiang et al. 2025 ) , further amplifies these risks for both original non-AI content, and AI-generated content. For original copyrighted content, prompt inversion can enable unauthorized reproduction. For AI-generated content, prompt inversion, also called prompt recovery or prompt stealing, can result in prompts that encode valuable creative knowledge and generation recipes. Some AI artists have refused to share their prompts see ( Colorado Public Radio 2023 ) . For both original and AI-generated content, the risk is recproducing the target image, or elements of a target image, as closely as possible. Beyond security concerns, prompt inversion is important for understanding model behavior, studying text-image alignment, and improving model transparency. Recovering prompts from generated images can support model provenance, attribution, and interpretable AI by exposing the semantic factors underlying image generation. Existing approaches span both white-box settings, where model parameters or gradients are available, and black-box settings, where access is restricted to APIs or generated outputs. Understanding how effectively prompts can be reconstructed in these settings is therefore critical for both advancing trustworthy AI and assessing emerging risks to intellectual property and content ownership. Per-region claims from the VLM are filtered by an evidence-gated Verifier , while counts and spatial relations are derived deterministically in the geometric extraction block (gray). The Composer serializes the surviving claims into the final prompt P ⁡ ( I ) P(I) , which the generator renders as G ⁡ ( P ⁡ ( I ) ) G(P(I)) . In white-box settings, prompt inversion is typically formulated as an optimization problem in either the text-embedding space or the diffusion latent space. These methods leverage the alignment between vision and language encoders to iteratively refine prompts toward a target image. Representative examples include PEZ ( Wen et al. 2023 ) , PH2P ( Mahajan et al. 2024 ) , and STEPs ( Qiu et al. 2025 ) -all optimization-based approaches. While effective at improving image similarity, optimization-based methods often produce prompts that drift away from natural language, yielding token sequences that are difficult for humans to interpret. Moreover, the discrete nature of language introduces a fundamental challenge, as textual prompts are inherently incompatible with conventional continuous optimization techniques. In black-box settings, there is no knowledge of model parameters and access is limited to APIs or generated images, prompt inversion is commonly approached through image captioning and vision-language models (VLMs). Methods based on BLIP ( Li et al. 2022 ) , CLIP-IG ( pharmapsychotic 2023 ) , and VLMs generate prompts directly from visual content by leveraging pretrained vision and language encoders. Although these approaches produce fluent and interpretable descriptions, the prompts aren’t optimized, and often lack mechanisms for verifying whether generated claims are actually supported by the image, reducing prompt fidelity. More recently, PromptStealer ( Shen et al. 2024 ) decomposed prompt stealing into subject and modifier recovery, using a fine-tuned captioning model to infer the subject and a multi-label detector to predict stylistic modifiers, while PromptMiner ( Li et al. 2025b ) proposed an RL-based framework that mines prompts from online marketplaces and learns to recover them through reinforcement learning, followed by fuzz-based optimization of stylistic modifiers. While promising, this approach relies on the same image generation model for both target and reconstructed images and use the same objective function for the RL optimization and metric computation, raising concerns about generator-specific overfitting and evaluation circularity. We propose a state-of-the-art black-box prompt inversion attack, PROVE , that is evidence-based, training-free, and not generator-specific. PROVE consists of four stages: grounded claim proposal using frozen vision-language models and open-vocabulary detection; evidence-gated verification, where each atomic claim must satisfy a label-anchored CLIP margin on its corresponding image region; geometric fact extraction, which deterministically derives counts and spatial relationships; and deterministic composition, which serializes verified claims into a fluent prompt.We show that PROVE’s generated prompts are SOTA on MS-COCO, Flickr30K, and Lexica (Figure 1 ), and that the proposed attack is robust to reasonable defenses.

sections.heading: Prompt inversion for text-to-image models.
sections.text: Prompt inversion recovers a textual description from a target image such that regenerating from that text reproduces the image. Two families exist. Soft inversion optimizes continuous pseudo-tokens that are appended to the model vocabulary, as in Textual Inversion ( Gal et al. 2022 ) and multi-concept customization ( Kumari et al. 2023 ) ; the recovered artifact is an embedding and is not human readable. Hard inversion instead returns discrete natural language. PEZ performs gradient-based optimization over discrete tokens to recover prompts that reproduce a target image ( Wen et al. 2023 ) . PH2P optimizes interpretable prompts directly from a target image through a delayed projection scheme and L-BFGS ( Mahajan et al. 2024 ) EDITOR initializes from a captioning model, refines in latent space, and decodes back to text ( Li et al. 2025a ) . VGD removes the need for gradients, pairing a language model with CLIP guidance to produce coherent, human-readable prompts ( Kim et al. 2025 ) . We additionally evaluate STEPS and PromptMiner ( Qiu et al. 2025 ; Li et al. 2025b ) . Captioning models such as BLIP-2 are commonly used as a fast approximate baseline for this task ( Williams et al. 2024 ) . We note that this line of work is distinct from latent inversion methods such as null-text and negative-prompt inversion ( Mokady et al. 2023 ; Miyake et al. 2025 ) , which recover a noise trajectory for editing rather than a textual artifact, therefore falls outside the threat model we consider. All of the hard inversion methods we evaluate take a source image as input and return text. They were developed for prompt engineering, data attribution, model provenance, and watermark validation, and their reported evaluations measure CLIP-space image and text similarity, distributional alignment between generations from the original and recovered prompts, and human judgments of interpretability ( Wen et al. 2023 ; Mahajan et al. 2024 ; Williams et al. 2024 ) . We repurpose them as measurement instruments and evaluate them against a criterion their original benchmarks do not report.

sections.heading: Inversion as a privacy threat.
sections.text: A smaller body of work already treats inversion adversarially. Prompt stealing attacks such as PromptStealer reconstruct the prompt behind a generated image in order to appropriate its style or content ( Shen et al. 2024 ) , and Ye et al. extend this threat across modalities with a unified cross-modal inversion approach ( Ye et al. 2025 ) . A parallel line of work targets the training data rather than the prompt: membership inference attacks determine whether an image was used in training ( Wu et al. 2022 ) , extraction and replication studies show that diffusion models memorize and regurgitate individual training examples ( Carlini et al. 2023 ; Somepalli et al. 2023 ) , and fine-tuning has been shown to amplify this risk ( Li et al. 2024 ) . ML-Doctor provides a complementary, holistic risk assessment of inference attacks against machine learning models ( Liu et al. 2022 ) . Across this literature the asset at risk is either the prompt or the training set, and the adversary is assumed to hold some privileged relationship to the model. Our threat model assumes neither.

The task of recovering the prompt used to generate an image is referred to in the literature as either prompt inversion or prompt stealing ,in both cases the objective is to produce a prompt that reproduces the target image. Existing methods also differ in their assumptions about model access ( Li et al. 2025b ; Shen et al. 2024 ) , framing the task as either white-box or black-box problem. White-box methods are gradient-based optimization approaches that require access to the model architecture and to the text and vision encoders. Black-box methods, in contrast, assume access only to the target image, with no access to the text-to-image generative model. Our method (Figure 2 ) is a black-box approach: given only the target image, the objective is to recover the prompt that generated it. In this work, we focus on the black-box setting, with particular emphasis on dense scenes.

sections.heading: Prompt Inversion
sections.text: Prior prompt-inversion methods fall into three families, gradient-based approaches optimize prompt embeddings against a CLIP or denoising objective ( Mahajan et al. 2024 ; Wen et al. 2023 ) making recovered prompts drift off the natural-language manifold and are often unreadable. Autoregressive approaches decode prompts with a captioner or language model ( Li et al. 2022 ; pharmapsychotic 2023 ) , producing readable and interpretable text where claims are never checked against the image. RL based approaches formulate prompt recovery as a Markov Decision Process (MDP), training a policy over prompt tokens with image-similarity rewards ( Li et al. 2025b ) optimizing against the scoring model invites both evaluation circularity and overfitting to a single generator. In contrast, our method is bottom-up and training-free, rather than optimizing token sequences or fine-tuning any model, we are composing the prompt from the scene’s content itself where detected instances, their attributes, and their spatial relations by simply using frozen, off-the-shelf VLMs. Further, we retain only those claims that pass an explicit per-claim verification test against the image. To capture the semantic context and its spatial relations, in this work we break the image into multiple segments S 1 , S 2 , … , S n S_{1},S_{2},\ldots,S_{n} . Each of these segments contributes toward the objective, where 𝒞 ⁡ ( I ) \mathcal{C}(I) denotes the visual features and 𝒞 ⁡ ( P ) \mathcal{C}(P) the textual features or claims asserted by the prompt. We then define our objective as precision- constrained recall maximization. In simple words, it means a prompt maximizes the recoverable evidence to regenerate the image: 𝒫 ⁡ ( I ) = arg ⁡ max ⁡ ℛ ⁡ ( I , P ) \mathcal{P}(I)=\arg\max\mathcal{R}(I;P) such that 𝒞 ⁡ ( P ) ⊆ 𝒞 ⁡ ( I ) \mathcal{C}(P)\subseteq\mathcal{C}(I) . To understand the composition and curation of the prompt, we divide the task in four stages (Algorithm 1 ). a) Grounded Claim Proposal b) Evidence Gated Verification c) Geometric Fact Extraction, and d) Prompt Composition.

sections.text: This part is exempted from evidenced gated verification, as this is a grounded deterministic mechanism. These facts are computed directly using the { ( b i , l i ) } \{(b_{i},l_{i})\} , using the deterministic assumptions. In this part, ground truth is the detector output itself. First, let us say that the count c ​ n ​ t cnt is given by 𝐜𝐧𝐭 l = | { o : l o = l } | \mathbf{cnt}_{l}=\bigl|\{\,o:l_{o}=l\,\}\bigr| , thus for each label, the tally of the detections is determined by the NMS or spatial dedup. For labels with n l ≥ 2 n_{l}\geq 2 the prose is directly used in the final prompt, which is determined at the composition level. The support relations 𝐫𝐞𝐥 𝐝 ​ ( o , u ) \mathbf{rel_{d}}(o,u) are then computed in the describer, post-verification, over the scene parts. More commonly, this is specifically a surface-band rule over the bounding boxes. Finally, we compute the inter instance spatial relations 𝐫𝐞𝐥 𝐬 ​ ( o , o ′ ) \mathbf{rel_{s}}(o,o^{\prime}) that bypasses the evidence gate by the design. The spatial relations are presented at a level where it is computed by sorting the object centroid, adjacent pairs in order to get the relations by normalized gap, and finally the holding of the object i.e, any instance whose assigned parts include a held-category label (eg: man on the left is holding the controller). Since the evidence gate designed on top of the CLIP, it is unable to capture the global fine-grained details, contrastive image-text models behave similar to the bag-of-words on counting and the spatial order ( Yuksekgonul et al. 2023 ; Basu et al. 2024 ) .

sections.heading: Prompt Composition
sections.text: This is the final stage for the construction of the prompt that we feed to text-to-image model. The composition stage is divided into two different parts: a) verified hierarchy, and b) deterministic serialisation. The verified hierarchy is a pair H ⁡ ( I ) = ⟨ global , instances ⟩ H(I)=\langle\textit{global},\,\textit{instances}\rangle . The enriched global text combines the caption c g c_{g} , verified scene attributes, counts, and injected relations where each instance carries its label, position tag, box, and kept claim-set K k K_{k} . This structure is auditable by construction where every claim is grounded and carries its evidence score. Text-to-image generators, however, are trained on flat text and cannot ingest hierarchy, so H ⁡ ( I ) H(I) must be linearized. This is the role of the deterministic composition operator μ \mu . It emits the global text first, then per-instance positional clauses, and finally a background clause for unowned scene objects. A repair pass removes dangling fragments and duplicate claims and rejoins the result into fluent sentences.

sections.heading: Experiments
sections.text: We design experiments to measure image recovery for original real images and AI-generated images. For the original real images domain, we use the MS-COCO ( Lin et al. 2014 ) and Flickr30K ( Plummer et al. 2015 ) datasets. MS-COCO and Flickr30K provide real photographs paired with human-written captions, and stress prompt recovery on dense, everyday scenes that contain multiple interacting objects, counts, and spatial relations, exactly the regime our per-claim evidence pipeline targets. For MS-COCO and Flickr30K a prompt is generated directly from original dataset images. For the generative-art domain, we use the Lexica ( Lexica 2024 ) dataset. Lexica consists of art-style images paired with the engineered prompts that produced them, and stresses recovery of the stylistic and aesthetic modifiers characteristic of prompt marketplaces. For Lexica, following prior work, we use the provided ground-truth prompt to generate an image, which in turn used to generate the inverted prompt. We use two state-of-the-art open-weight text-to-image models both to render recovered prompts back into images and, where noted above, to construct the target images: FLUX.1-dev ( Labs et al. 2025 ) and Stable Diffusion 3.5 Large ( Esser et al. 2024 ) . Each method is evaluated independently using both generators. Crucially, the generator is used only to render images for evaluation and is applied identically to all methods. We compare against seven prompt-inversion methods drawn from the three established families. Optimization-based: PH2P ( Mahajan et al. 2024 ) , STEPS ( Qiu et al. 2025 ) , and VGD ( Kim et al. 2025 ) , which recover prompts by gradient-based or guided search against a similarity objective. Captioning-based: BLIP ( Li et al. 2022 ) , CLIP-Interrogator (CLIP-IG) ( pharmapsychotic 2023 ) , and a strong VLM-as-expert baseline that prompts a frozen vision-language model to describe the image directly. RL-based: PromptMiner ( Li et al. 2025b ) , which learns a prompt-recovery policy via reinforcement learning with fuzz-based modifier optimization. All methods take a single source image as input and return text. Since prompt inversion is ultimately judged by whether the recovered prompt reproduces the target, we report metrics comparing the resulting image to the target image: DINO ( ↑ \uparrow ), the cosine similarity of self-supervised DINO features; LPIPS ( ↓ \downarrow ), a learned perceptual distance, and CLIP ( ↑ \uparrow ), the CLIP-space cosine similarity between the recovered prompt and the target image (text-image alignment). Reporting a semantic image measure (DINO), a perceptual image measure (LPIPS), and a text-image alignment measure (CLIP) guards against any single metric being gamed by an off-manifold or degenerate prompt. All generations are done twice using two seeds, and average metrics of the two generations are reported. As shown in Table 1 , PROVE achieves the strongest overall image recovery across all three datasets, with qualitative reconstructions in Figure 3 confirming that it recovers object counts and spatial layout more faithfully than the baselines.

sections.heading: Results.
sections.text: Table 1 reports image-similarity metrics across 100 randomly selected images from each of the three datasets, across two text-to-image generators ( FLUX.1-dev and Stable Diffusion 3.5 Large ). PROVE is compared against seven state-of-the-art white-box and black-box methods. PROVE provides new state-of-the-art results. While Table 1 presented aggregate quantitative results for 600 images across the three datasets and two generators, Figure 3 presents sample qualitative examples from the three datasets. Additional examples are provided in the supplementary material.

sections.heading: Robustness and Defenses
sections.text: Because prompt inversion can be misused, we evaluate PROVE under defenses an image owner might deploy: three post-hoc perturbations from prior work ( Shen et al. 2024 ) such as Noise Injection , Puzzle , and Watermarking , as well as a stronger white-box defense, Adversarial CLIP , which perturbs the image against the CLIP encoder while leaving it perceptually intact. Results are reported in Table 2 . Noise Injection adds zero-mean Gaussian noise to the target before inversion, degrading low-level statistics without altering scene content, and thus probes whether inversion depends on precise pixel appearance, a method whose information flows through semantic channels (captioning, detection, region description) should be unaffected, whereas one keyed to fine texture should degrade. Puzzle divides the image into a 4 × 4 4\times 4 grid and randomly offsets each patch, disrupting global spatial coherence while leaving local content intact. It perturbs scene composition rather than appearance and so tests our geometric-fact channel, where object identity survives within patches, so counts persist, while support and relation predicates, computed from box coordinates, are most exposed to the displacement. Watermarking puts semi-transparent text across the image. Unlike the previous two, it adds content rather than removing it, probing whether verification suppresses inserted content lacking a grounded visual reference. Following the white-box formulation of ( Shen et al. 2024 ) , Adversarial CLIP applies iterative FGSM to the CLIP image encoder, minimizing cosine similarity between perturbed and clean embeddings within an L ∞ L_{\infty} ball ( ϵ = 8 / 255 \epsilon=8/255 , 100 steps) – the standard bound in the adversarial-robustness literature, at which the perturbation is imperceptible in natural images. Prior inversion methods score, search, and evaluate through the same encoder, so the perturbation corrupts their objective end to end. Our decomposition into a CLIP-free proposal stage and a CLIP-guided verification stage confines the effect to the verification gate alone: the VLM and detector channels are unaffected, and unverified claims fall back to their object labels. sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: We propose PROVE , a training-free, optimization-free prompt inversion (prompt stealing) method that recovers the prompt used to generate a target image. PROVE proceeds in four stages. First, a frozen VLM and open-vocabulary detection propose fine-grained atomic claims about the image. Second, each claim is retained only if it satisfies a label-anchored CLIP margin on its corresponding region. Third, counts and spatial relations are derived deterministically from the detections rather than asserted by the VLM. Finally, the verified claims are serialized into a single fluent prompt, with no generator in the loop. PROVE recovers more descriptive and accurate prompts than the considered baselines. These gains come from verification and deterministic derivation, without any training, optimization, or access to the target generator. While this constitutes a stronger prompt-stealing attack, with direct implications for copyright and the reproduction of content, our pipeline verifies visual content while, by construction, refusing artist and platform attribution, separating faithful description from unauthorized reproduction of an artist’s identity. PROVE reports visual evidence without asserting authorship. We hope this separation of description from identity offers a useful reference point for studying copyright concerns.

sections.heading: Models.
sections.text: All components are frozen, off-the-shelf models; PROVE requires no training or gradient optimization. We use Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct as the vision-language model (VLM) g ϕ g_{\phi} for global captioning, scene-attribute extraction, object inventory, and per-region slot-schema description. Open-vocabulary detection D θ D_{\theta} uses OWLv2 (ViT-B/16, ensemble), and the evidence gate E E scores claims with CLIP ViT-L/14. Region proposals are deduplicated with non-maximum suppression at an IoU threshold of 0.5 0.5 .

sections.heading: Pipeline configuration.
sections.text: Detection runs on a 512 × 512 512\times 512 working copy, while all region crops are taken at native resolution to preserve fine detail; crops are padded by a factor p = 0.2 p=0.2 of the box dimensions. The evidence margin is δ = 0.03 \delta=0.03 : a claim c c over region x i x_{i} with label ℓ i \ell_{i} is retained if and only if f ⁡ ( x i , c ) ≥ f ⁡ ( x i , ℓ i ) − δ f(x_{i},c)\geq f(x_{i},\ell_{i})-\delta , i.e., it must match the crop at least as well as the bare object label up to the margin. Claims failing the gate fall back to their object label, and multi-clause claims are salvaged clause-by-clause before rejection. Geometric facts (counts, support, and spatial relations) are derived deterministically from detection boxes and bypass the evidence gate. sections.text: Recovered prompts are rendered with FLUX.1-dev and SD3.5-Large under identical sampling settings ( T T inference steps, guidance scale g g , fixed seeds { s 1 , s 2 } \{s_{1},s_{2}\} ) for all methods, so differences reflect the prompt rather than the generator. As prompt marketplaces emerge, recovered prompts can enable both the unauthorized reproduction and redistribution of copyrighted creative works, and the exposure of the prompts that encode an artist’s creative recipe in AI-generated content. Existing prompt inversion methods rely on gradient-based optimization, autoregressive captioning, or reinforcement learning. However, optimization-based methods often produce unreadable prompts, captioning methods hallucinate unverified details, and RL-based approaches frequently overfit to specific generators while introducing evaluation circularity. We introduce PROVE (Prompt Recovery with Verified Evidence), a training-free, black-box prompt inversion attack that reconstructs prompts by composing verifiable scene descriptions rather than optimizing token sequences, targeting both original copyrighted works and AI-generated content. The resulting prompts are fully auditable, with every recovered claim grounded in explicit image evidence, and are formalized through a precision-constrained recall maximization objective. Across MS-COCO, Flickr30K, and Lexica, using state-of-the-art text-to-image generators, PROVE consistently outperforms optimization, captioning, and RL-based baselines on image similarity (DINO, LPIPS) and text-image alignment (CLIP), without any training, generator access, or fine-tuning, demonstrating a stronger and more practical prompt inversion attack. Department of Computer Science, Georgetown University Introduction Text-to-image generation has been transformed by diffusion- and flow-based models such as Stable Diffusion ( Esser et al. 2024 ) , DALL-E ( Ramesh et al. 2021 ) , FLUX ( Labs et al. 2025 ) , and Imagen ( Saharia et al. 2022 ) . These models can synthesize highly realistic images from natural-language descriptions, with image quality and fidelity largely determined by their ability to interpret user prompts. This capability has democratized image creation, editing, and content generation, enabling non-experts to produce sophisticated visual content through simple textual instructions. However, the same accessibility introduces significant security, safety, and intellectual property concerns. Prompt manipulation and adversarial prompting can facilitate harmful generation, including the creation of copyrighted derivatives and other forms of misuse ( Bariach et al. 2024 ) . The emergence of prompt marketplaces, where carefully engineered prompts are shared or sold ( Shen et al. 2024 ; Jiang et al. 2025 ) , further amplifies these risks for both original non-AI content, and AI-generated content. For original copyrighted content, prompt inversion can enable unauthorized reproduction. For AI-generated content, prompt inversion, also called prompt recovery or prompt stealing, can result in prompts that encode valuable creative knowledge and generation recipes. Some AI artists have refused to share their prompts see ( Colorado Public Radio 2023 ) . For both original and AI-generated content, the risk is recproducing the target image, or elements of a target image, as closely as possible. Beyond security concerns, prompt inversion is important for understanding model behavior, studying text-image alignment, and improving model transparency. Recovering prompts from generated images can support model provenance, attribution, and interpretable AI by exposing the semantic factors underlying image generation. Existing approaches span both white-box settings, where model parameters or gradients are available, and black-box settings, where access is restricted to APIs or generated outputs. Understanding how effectively prompts can be reconstructed in these settings is therefore critical for both advancing trustworthy AI and assessing emerging risks to intellectual property and content ownership. In white-box settings, prompt inversion is typically formulated as an optimization problem in either the text-embedding space or the diffusion latent space. These methods leverage the alignment between vision and language encoders to iteratively refine prompts toward a target image. Representative examples include PEZ ( Wen et al. 2023 ) , PH2P ( Mahajan et al. 2024 ) , and STEPs ( Qiu et al. 2025 ) -all optimization-based approaches. While effective at improving image similarity, optimization-based methods often produce prompts that drift away from natural language, yielding token sequences that are difficult for humans to interpret. Moreover, the discrete nature of language introduces a fundamental challenge, as textual prompts are inherently incompatible with conventional continuous optimization techniques. In black-box settings, there is no knowledge of model parameters and access is limited to APIs or generated images, prompt inversion is commonly approached through image captioning and vision-language models (VLMs). Methods based on BLIP ( Li et al. 2022 ) , CLIP-IG ( pharmapsychotic 2023 ) , and VLMs generate prompts directly from visual content by leveraging pretrained vision and language encoders. Although these approaches produce fluent and interpretable descriptions, the prompts aren’t optimized, and often lack mechanisms for verifying whether generated claims are actually supported by the image, reducing prompt fidelity. More recently, PromptStealer ( Shen et al. 2024 ) decomposed prompt stealing into subject and modifier recovery, using a fine-tuned captioning model to infer the subject and a multi-label detector to predict stylistic modifiers, while PromptMiner ( Li et al. 2025b ) proposed an RL-based framework that mines prompts from online marketplaces and learns to recover them through reinforcement learning, followed by fuzz-based optimization of stylistic modifiers. While promising, this approach relies on the same image generation model for both target and reconstructed images and use the same objective function for the RL optimization and metric computation, raising concerns about generator-specific overfitting and evaluation circularity. We propose a state-of-the-art black-box prompt inversion attack, PROVE , that is evidence-based, training-free, and not generator-specific. PROVE consists of four stages: grounded claim proposal using frozen vision-language models and open-vocabulary detection; evidence-gated verification, where each atomic claim must satisfy a label-anchored CLIP margin on its corresponding image region; geometric fact extraction, which deterministically derives counts and spatial relationships; and deterministic composition, which serializes verified claims into a fluent prompt.We show that PROVE’s generated prompts are SOTA on MS-COCO, Flickr30K, and Lexica (Figure 1 ), and that the proposed attack is robust to reasonable defenses. Related Work Prompt inversion for text-to-image models. Prompt inversion recovers a textual description from a target image such that regenerating from that text reproduces the image. Two families exist. Soft inversion optimizes continuous pseudo-tokens that are appended to the model vocabulary, as in Textual Inversion ( Gal et al. 2022 ) and multi-concept customization ( Kumari et al. 2023 ) ; the recovered artifact is an embedding and is not human readable. Hard inversion instead returns discrete natural language. PEZ performs gradient-based optimization over discrete tokens to recover prompts that reproduce a target image ( Wen et al. 2023 ) . PH2P optimizes interpretable prompts directly from a target image through a delayed projection scheme and L-BFGS ( Mahajan et al. 2024 ) EDITOR initializes from a captioning model, refines in latent space, and decodes back to text ( Li et al. 2025a ) . VGD removes the need for gradients, pairing a language model with CLIP guidance to produce coherent, human-readable prompts ( Kim et al. 2025 ) . We additionally evaluate STEPS and PromptMiner ( Qiu et al. 2025 ; Li et al. 2025b ) . Captioning models such as BLIP-2 are commonly used as a fast approximate baseline for this task ( Williams et al. 2024 ) . We note that this line of work is distinct from latent inversion methods such as null-text and negative-prompt inversion ( Mokady et al. 2023 ; Miyake et al. 2025 ) , which recover a noise trajectory for editing rather than a textual artifact, therefore falls outside the threat model we consider. All of the hard inversion methods we evaluate take a source image as input and return text. They were developed for prompt engineering, data attribution, model provenance, and watermark validation, and their reported evaluations measure CLIP-space image and text similarity, distributional alignment between generations from the original and recovered prompts, and human judgments of interpretability ( Wen et al. 2023 ; Mahajan et al. 2024 ; Williams et al. 2024 ) . We repurpose them as measurement instruments and evaluate them against a criterion their original benchmarks do not report. Inversion as a privacy threat. A smaller body of work already treats inversion adversarially. Prompt stealing attacks such as PromptStealer reconstruct the prompt behind a generated image in order to appropriate its style or content ( Shen et al. 2024 ) , and Ye et al. extend this threat across modalities with a unified cross-modal inversion approach ( Ye et al. 2025 ) . A parallel line of work targets the training data rather than the prompt: membership inference attacks determine whether an image was used in training ( Wu et al. 2022 ) , extraction and replication studies show that diffusion models memorize and regurgitate individual training examples ( Carlini et al. 2023 ; Somepalli et al. 2023 ) , and fine-tuning has been shown to amplify this risk ( Li et al. 2024 ) . ML-Doctor provides a complementary, holistic risk assessment of inference attacks against machine learning models ( Liu et al. 2022 ) . Across this literature the asset at risk is either the prompt or the training set, and the adversary is assumed to hold some privileged relationship to the model. Our threat model assumes neither. The task of recovering the prompt used to generate an image is referred to in the literature as either prompt inversion or prompt stealing ,in both cases the objective is to produce a prompt that reproduces the target image. Existing methods also differ in their assumptions about model access ( Li et al. 2025b ; Shen et al. 2024 ) , framing the task as either white-box or black-box problem. White-box methods are gradient-based optimization approaches that require access to the model architecture and to the text and vision encoders. Black-box methods, in contrast, assume access only to the target image, with no access to the text-to-image generative model. Our method (Figure 2 ) is a black-box approach: given only the target image, the objective is to recover the prompt that generated it. In this work, we focus on the black-box setting, with particular emphasis on dense scenes. Prompt Inversion Prior prompt-inversion methods fall into three families, gradient-based approaches optimize prompt embeddings against a CLIP or denoising objective ( Mahajan et al. 2024 ; Wen et al. 2023 ) making recovered prompts drift off the natural-language manifold and are often unreadable. Autoregressive approaches decode prompts with a captioner or language model ( Li et al. 2022 ; pharmapsychotic 2023 ) , producing readable and interpretable text where claims are never checked against the image. RL based approaches formulate prompt recovery as a Markov Decision Process (MDP), training a policy over prompt tokens with image-similarity rewards ( Li et al. 2025b ) optimizing against the scoring model invites both evaluation circularity and overfitting to a single generator. In contrast, our method is bottom-up and training-free, rather than optimizing token sequences or fine-tuning any model, we are composing the prompt from the scene’s content itself where detected instances, their attributes, and their spatial relations by simply using frozen, off-the-shelf VLMs. Further, we retain only those claims that pass an explicit per-claim verification test against the image. To capture the semantic context and its spatial relations, in this work we break the image into multiple segments S 1 , S 2 , … , S n S_{1},S_{2},\ldots,S_{n} . Each of these segments contributes toward the objective, where 𝒞 ⁡ ( I ) \mathcal{C}(I) denotes the visual features and 𝒞 ⁡ ( P ) \mathcal{C}(P) the textual features or claims asserted by the prompt. We then define our objective as precision- constrained recall maximization. Experiments We design experiments to measure image recovery for original real images and AI-generated images. For the original real images domain, we use the MS-COCO ( Lin et al. 2014 ) and Flickr30K ( Plummer et al. 2015 ) datasets. MS-COCO and Flickr30K provide real photographs paired with human-written captions, and stress prompt recovery on dense, everyday scenes that contain multiple interacting objects, counts, and spatial relations, exactly the regime our per-claim evidence pipeline targets. For MS-COCO and Flickr30K a prompt is generated directly from original dataset images. For the generative-art domain, we use the Lexica ( Lexica 2024 ) dataset. Lexica consists of art-style images paired with the engineered prompts that produced them, and stresses recovery of the stylistic and aesthetic modifiers characteristic of prompt marketplaces. For Lexica, following prior work, we use the provided ground-truth prompt to generate an image, which in turn used to generate the inverted prompt. We use two state-of-the-art open-weight text-to-image models both to render recovered prompts back into images and, where noted above, to construct the target images: FLUX.1-dev ( Labs et al. 2025 ) and Stable Diffusion 3.5 Large ( Esser et al. 2024 ) . Each method is evaluated independently using both generators. Crucially, the generator is used only to render images for evaluation and is applied identically to all methods. We compare against seven prompt-inversion methods drawn from the three established families. Optimization-based: PH2P ( Mahajan et al. 2024 ) , STEPS ( Qiu et al. 2025 ) , and VGD ( Kim et al. 2025 ) , which recover prompts by gradient-based or guided search against a similarity objective. Captioning-based: BLIP ( Li et al. 2022 ) , CLIP-Interrogator (CLIP-IG) ( pharmapsychotic 2023 ) , and a strong VLM-as-expert baseline that prompts a frozen vision-language model to describe the image directly. All methods take a single source image as input and return text. Robustness and Defenses Because prompt inversion can be misused, we evaluate PROVE under defenses an image owner might deploy: three post-hoc perturbations from prior work ( Shen et al. 2024 ) such as Noise Injection , Puzzle , and Watermarking , as well as a stronger white-box defense, Adversarial CLIP , which perturbs the image against the CLIP encoder while leaving it perceptually intact. Results are reported in Table 2 . Noise Injection adds zero-mean Gaussian noise to the target before inversion, degrading low-level statistics without altering scene content, and thus probes whether inversion depends on precise pixel appearance, a method whose information flows through semantic channels (captioning, detection, region description) should be unaffected, whereas one keyed to fine texture should degrade. Puzzle divides the image into a 4 × 4 4	imes 4 grid and randomly offsets each patch, disrupting global spatial coherence while leaving local content intact. It perturbs scene composition rather than appearance and so tests our geometric-fact channel, where object identity survives within patches, so counts persist, while support and relation predicates, computed from box coordinates, are most exposed to the displacement. Watermarking puts semi-transparent text across the image. Unlike the previous two, it adds content rather than removing it, probing whether verification suppresses inserted content lacking a grounded visual reference. Following the white-box formulation of ( Shen et al. 2024 ) , Adversarial CLIP applies iterative FGSM to the CLIP image encoder, minimizing cosine similarity between perturbed and clean embeddings within an L ∞ L_{\infty} ball ( ϵ = 8 / 255 \epsilon=8/255 , 100 steps) – the standard bound in the adversarial-robustness literature, at which the perturbation is imperceptible in natural images. Prior inversion methods score, search, and evaluate through the same encoder, so the perturbation corrupts their objective end to end. Our decomposition into a CLIP-free proposal stage and a CLIP-guided verification stage confines the effect to the verification gate alone: the VLM and detector channels are unaffected, and unverified claims fall back to their object labels. CLIP 0.720 0.570 0.843 Conclusion We propose PROVE , a training-free, optimization-free prompt inversion (prompt stealing) method that recovers the prompt used to generate a target image. PROVE proceeds in four stages. First, a frozen VLM and open-vocabulary detection propose fine-grained atomic claims about the image. Second, each claim is retained only if it satisfies a label-anchored CLIP margin on its corresponding region. Third, counts and spatial relations are derived deterministically from the detections rather than asserted by the VLM. Finally, the verified claims are serialized into a single fluent prompt, with no generator in the loop. PROVE recovers more descriptive and accurate prompts than the considered baselines. These gains come from verification and deterministic derivation, without any training, optimization, or access to the target generator. While this constitutes a stronger prompt-stealing attack, with direct implications for copyright and the reproduction of content, our pipeline verifies visual content while, by construction, refusing artist and platform attribution, separating faithful description from unauthorized reproduction of an artist’s identity. PROVE reports visual evidence without asserting authorship. We hope this separation of description from identity offers a useful reference point for studying copyright concerns.
